principles.principle: Findings are reported by making a specific table, column, row, panel, or figure the grammatical subject or opening anchor of the sentence ('Table V shows...', 'Row 4 of Table VI shows...', 'Panel A of Table III demonstrates...') rather than stating the result free-floating.
principles.why: Pointing each claim at the exact exhibit lets the reader verify it instantly and keeps a dense run of numbers navigable; the table does the showing, so the prose stays a guided tour of the evidence instead of a recitation of figures.

principles.principle: The atomic unit pairs a bare statistical fact (a coefficient's sign and significance) with an immediate interpretive clause that converts it into substantive meaning, typically hinged on 'which suggests', 'indicates that', 'is consistent with', or 'as predicted by [the] hypothesis'.
principles.why: Welding the number to its meaning in a single breath spares the reader the translation work and keeps the statistics tethered to the paper's argument, so each result lands as a point rather than a data dump.

principles.principle: Coefficients are converted into tangible, everyday units — basis points, percentage points, dollars, counts per year — and frequently set against an explicit benchmark so the reader can judge whether the effect is large.
principles.why: Concrete units plus a yardstick turn an abstract estimate into something the reader can feel the size of, which is what lets these papers credibly call an effect 'economically significant' rather than merely statistically detectable.

principles.principle: Authors narrate their own analytic actions in the first person ('we find', 'we estimate', 'I use', 'we next examine', 're-estimate'), presenting the results as a procedure they walk the reader through rather than as disembodied facts.
principles.why: The visible 'we/I + action verb' frames findings as deliberate, accountable choices, builds trust in the method, and turns a list of estimates into a guided narrative with forward momentum.

principles.device: Raise the rival, then refute it
principles.principle: The prose deliberately voices a competing interpretation or data concern on the reader's behalf ('One possible concern...', 'One alternative interpretation...', 'it is possible that...') and then dismantles it, usually by deploying an additional test, control, or placebo.
principles.why: By doing the skeptic's objecting for them and answering on the spot, the writing closes off escape routes and stages the results as the survivor of an adversarial process rather than a single fragile correlation.

principles.principle: Claims are voiced through soft epistemic verbs ('suggest', 'appear', 'seem') and then explicitly bounded by the authors themselves, who concede the limits of their evidence ('only suggestive', 'we should not overstate', 'we do not want to push too far').
principles.why: Calibrated tentativeness pre-empts the charge of overclaiming and signals that the authors see the weaknesses before a referee does, which paradoxically makes the surviving claims more credible.

principles.principle: The section advances as an explicitly marked tour: ordinal and enumerated markers ('First,... Second,...', '(i)... (ii)...') step through specifications, and findings are stitched and closed with stance-and-summary adverbials fronting sentences ('Interestingly,...', 'Overall,...', 'Taken together,...').
principles.why: The verbal scaffolding tells the reader where they are in the argument and how to weigh each item, so a long parade of regressions reads as an ordered, cumulative case instead of an undifferentiated heap.

redteam_rejected.reason: Conflates two distinct devices that the other two agents correctly keep separate: 'anticipate-and-refute a rival' (a1-p5, a3-p6) and 'hedge/self-limit verbs' (a1-p7, a3-p5). Its evidence splits across both — bertrand_schoar2003 ('one might worry that...') and thewissen2024 ('it is possible that...') show rival-raising, while harford1999 ('suggests...may'), dwz ('suggest'), and lm2011 ('We should not overstate') show hedging — so it names no single underlying device and cannot be cleanly folded into either group. Both halves already survive as distinct canonical principles (a3-p6 and a3-p5), so nothing is lost by dropping it.

side_notes: Coverage gap: all three agents operated at the sentence/clause level. The section-level architecture of a results section — how subsections are ordered (headline result first vs. cumulative build-up) and how one paragraph transitions into the next — was left unexamined by all three; only within-paragraph ordinal signposting (group a2-p4) was captured.

Coverage gap: verb tense/aspect as a stylistic convention — the uniform reporting-present-tense seen across the evidence ('Table V shows', 'the probability...increases', 'I estimate') — recurs throughout but was never isolated as a device by any agent.

Coverage gap: sentence-length cadence/rhythm (the alternation between short one-line verdict sentences and long multi-clause result-plus-gloss sentences) was not examined; every named device concerns sentence content or framing, none concern pacing.
